title: Appreciating the scope and dimensions of “surcharge” in taxation laws: Implications of Supreme Court’s larger Bench exposition on “surcharge” and “cess”
summary: Introduction Tax on tax is economically frowned upon as it results into cascading effect. Whether such economic distortion can render the levy legally invalid is a different matter altogether. Giving short thrift to the debate, about five decades back the Supreme Court observed that “bad economics may be good law and vice versa ”, thereby.

note.Facts: Arjun Flour Mills challenged a State levy that computed a surcharge on the sales-tax payable by a dealer, arguing it was in substance a tax on the dealer’s income and beyond State competence. The State contended it was merely a “surcharge” – an enhancement of the sales-tax rate.
note.Issue: Whether a levy that is computed as a percentage of the sales-tax payable is a valid surcharge (i.e., a sales-tax) or an unconstitutional tax on income/fiscal burden of the dealer.
note.Held: The Supreme Court held that the levy is a surcharge – an enhancement of the principal sales-tax – and therefore a valid sales-tax, not a tax on income. Consequently, while the surcharge is constitutionally valid, the Court barred States from levying it post-GST transition because the underlying sales-tax statutes have ceased to exist.
note.Principle: A surcharge, even if computed on the amount of another tax, retains the character of the principal levy; the method of computation does not alter the subject-matter of the tax.
note.Provisions: - Arjun Flour Mills v. State of Odisha (larger Bench) – cited. - State of Telangana v. Tirumala Construction – GST transition provision, Sec. 19, Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016. - No specific statutory sections were quoted for the surcharge itself; the decision refers to the constitutional entry on “tax on sale or purchase of goods”.
note.Exam angle: Constitutional Law – State List (List II) power to tax sale or purchase of goods.* The question can be framed as: “Explain the scope of ‘surcharge’ under State taxation power and its limitation post-GST (Sec. 19, 101st Amendment).” This tests understanding of legislative competence, the distinction between surcharge and cess, and the effect of the GST transition on State levies.

title: Supreme Court Quashes Mining Land Acquisition In Tribal Area, Holds Gram Sabha Consent Mandatory
summary: The Court held that Section 41(3) of the RFCTLARR Act was mandatory for acquisitions in scheduled areas.

note.Facts: The government sought to acquire land in scheduled village areas of Sundergarhi district, Odisha, for a Dalmia Cement plant, but the gram panchayats had rejected the proposal and no consent was recorded on Form M as required.
note.Issue: Whether prior consent of the gram panchayat/gram sabha under Section 41(3) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 is mandatory for land acquisition in scheduled areas, and whether its absence vitiates the acquisition.
note.Held: The Supreme Court set aside the acquisition proceedings, holding that the consent requirement under Section 41(3) is mandatory, not directory, and its non-compliance renders the acquisition void.
note.Principle: For land acquisition in scheduled areas, the statutory requirement of obtaining gram sabha consent under Section 41(3) of the 2013 Act is mandatory; failure to secure it cannot be cured later and invalidates the acquisition.
note.Provisions: Section 41(3), 2013 Act; Section 2(2)(b), 2013 Act (80% family consent for private company); Rule 41, Odisha Rules (Form M); Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (mining lease).
note.Exam angle: Test on the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition Act, 2013 – focus on mandatory consent under Section 41(3) and its applicability to private-company projects in scheduled areas.

title: Top Legal Developments [9-15 Nov 2026]: Digital Arrest Scams, GST, AI Deepfakes and More
summary: This week witnessed significant judicial developments, with the Supreme Court calling for mandatory compensation to victims of cyber frauds where financial institutions fail to exercise due diligence, and clarifying when balance sheet entries can extend the limitation period. The High Courts delivered key rulings on GST input tax credit, AI-generated deepfakes, personality rights, social media.

note.Facts: A three-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court examined digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds where victims lost money because their banks failed to exercise due diligence.
note.Issue: Whether financial institutions are required to compensate victims when cyber fraud occurs due to their lack of due diligence.
note.Held: The Court directed that banks must indemnify victims and pay compensation not less than the amount lost, and must adopt preventive safeguards such as suspending suspicious transactions, notifying police and physically verifying transactions.
note.Principle: A financial institution that fails to exercise due diligence and thereby enables a cyber fraud must compensate the victim for the full loss.
note.Exam angle: Likely framed under the Banking Regulation Act / RBI regulatory framework, testing the duty of banks to exercise due diligence and the remedy of mandatory compensation for cyber-fraud victims.

'Pathetic Reality, Collective Shame': Delhi High Court Condemns Dowry Harassment, Deaths Of Married Women
case_name: Chhotey Lal & Jai Dev v. State
summary: The Court noted that when the bride's family is unable to fulfil such demands, the harassment may continue, sometimes resulting in her death, suicide or divorce. In other instances, women continue to endure cruel treatment while suppressing their emotions.

note.Facts: The appellant husband and his family were convicted for the death of his wife, who set herself on fire in 2001 after alleged dowry harassment for a motorcycle, gas stove, water motor and ₹25,000.
note.Issue: Whether the prosecution proved cruelty or dowry harassment sufficient to sustain a conviction under Section 304B (dowry death) and whether the husband’s conduct amounted to cruelty under Section 498A.
note.Held: The Court held that the prosecution failed to prove dowry-related cruelty required for Section 304B, converting the dowry-death conviction to abetment of suicide under Section 306, while upholding the conviction under Section 498A for cruelty. The father and brother were acquitted.
note.Principle: A conviction under Section 304B IPC demands proof of cruelty linked to dowry demands immediately before death; absent such proof, the charge cannot stand, though persistent matrimonial cruelty can sustain a conviction under Section 498A and, if it leads to suicide, under Section 306.
note.Provisions: Sections 498A, 304B, 306 IPC (as cited in the judgment).
note.Exam angle: Questions may test the application of IPC Sections 498A, 304B and 306 in dowry-related cases, focusing on the evidentiary requirement of a direct link between dowry demand and death and the distinction between cruelty and dowry death.
